extracted.intended_audience: naturalists, evolutionary biologists, scholars and educated general readers interested in inheritance and sexual selection
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and applying Darwin's principles about how the timing of character development and sexual selection affect whether traits are transmitted to one sex or both, and summarizing empirical observations on sex ratios across species. Useful for analysing hypotheses about sex-limited traits, secondary sexual characters, and population sex-ratio patterns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing of development predicts sex-limited inheritance
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters developed at a late period of life in one sex tend to be transmitted to that same sex alone; characters developed at an early period tend to be transmitted to both sexes (though this converse rule is less general).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin gives numerous examples: horns in many deer and antelopes appear late and are often male-limited, whereas horns in reindeer appear very early and in both sexes. Spurs, plumes and wing specula that appear early are often common to both sexes. Note exceptions exist and the rule is not absolute.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sexual selection acts only after reproductive age, mostly on males
rubrics_metrics.description: Sexual selection cannot operate before the age for reproduction; due to greater ardour and rivalry in males it generally acts more on males than females, producing weapons, holding-organs, and ornaments related to acquiring mates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains why many secondary sexual characters arise at or after maturity and why adult males often differ markedly from young males. Examples include horns, spurs, and ornamental plumage. Consider interaction with natural selection (e.g., conspicuous traits may be disfavoured before reproductive age).

rubrics_metrics.name: Adult male characters often arise near reproductive age and are absent in young males
rubrics_metrics.description: Adult males frequently differ from young males because the successive variations that produced adult male characters typically arose near the age of reproduction; young males therefore often resemble females until later moults or development.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: young males of some ducks and pheasants resemble females until a later moult; Orthoptera and crustaceans show characters appearing at successive moults. This helps explain why conspicuous sexual characters are delayed until adulthood.

rubrics_metrics.name: Late-appearing variations transmitted to one sex accumulate by sexual selection
rubrics_metrics.description: Variations that appear late in life and are transmitted to the same sex alone are especially liable to be taken advantage of and accumulated by sexual selection in relation to reproduction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such traits, being useful for competition or attraction at reproductive age, are preserved and exaggerated (e.g., male weapons and ornaments). If analogous variations arose in females they would often not be preserved unless transmitted to males as well.

rubrics_metrics.name: Early-appearing variations tend to be transmitted to both sexes and are less often sex-limited
rubrics_metrics.description: When variations arise early in life they commonly become common to both sexes, especially if the sexes differ little in constitution during early development.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include horn development in reindeer and early-developing crest or speculum colours in some birds. However, the rule has exceptions (some congenital traits are sex-limited).

rubrics_metrics.name: Domestication and breed history modulate inheritance patterns
rubrics_metrics.description: In domesticated breeds the presence or absence of characters (e.g., horns) is often not firmly fixed; domestication can produce irregularities in sex-limited transmission and may yield intermediate or variable states.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: merino sheep with rams usually horned but some ewes horned and some rams hornless; pigeon and fowl sub-breeds where both sexes change colour during moults. Domestication can break or blur the patterns seen in wild species.

rubrics_metrics.name: Some congenital/embryonic traits can be sex-limited
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain abnormalities or congenital traits (e.g., supernumerary digits, absent phalanges, proclivity to bleeding, possibly colour-blindness) are determined very early embryonically yet may nevertheless be limited to one sex.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This observation shows that the early/late-development rule has notable exceptions and implies there must be some sexual difference even at very early embryonic stages. Gout is discussed as a case where adult-caused disease shows sex-limited transmission patterns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correlation between development timing and cranial/head protuberances in birds
rubrics_metrics.description: Dr. W. Marshall’s conclusion cited: protuberances confined to males are developed late in life, whereas those common to both sexes are developed very early.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin treats this as striking confirmation of his two rules. Examples include crests and bony skull protuberances in various fowl breeds and pheasants; spurs on peafowl develop later when male-limited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inheritance modes and outcomes are complex and not fixed
rubrics_metrics.description: Successive modifications in a species may be transmitted in different ways—some to one sex, some to both, some at particular ages—because the laws of inheritance and the causes of variability are extremely complex.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin warns that although timing of development is an important cause, it is not the sole cause. Expect many contingencies: interactions of sexual selection, natural selection, variation timing, and chance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiple factors influence proportional numbers of the sexes (sex ratios)
rubrics_metrics.description: The proportion of males to females varies across species and human populations and is influenced by many factors: season, parental ages, social and economic conditions, residence (rural/urban), immigration/crossing, and possibly polygamy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin compiles data: humans in England ~104.5 males per 100 females; variations across regions and nations; race-horses ~99.7:100; greyhounds ~110.1:100; sheep ~97.7:100 (at castration age). He emphasizes data are imperfect and affected by sample size and recording methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Higher male prenatal and early-life mortality affects observed sex ratios
rubrics_metrics.description: Male foetuses and infants have higher rates of stillbirth and early mortality (e.g., more still-born males and higher first-year male mortality), which influences population sex ratios despite greater male births at conception or birth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin cites statistics (e.g., still-born male excess, 126 boys die per 100 girls in first year in England) and suggests causes such as greater variability/defective development in males and larger head size causing birth complications. These demographic processes must be considered when interpreting birth ratios.

rubrics_metrics.name: Species- and breed-specific empirical sex-ratio data require cautious interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: Reported sex ratios for domestic and wild species (race-horses, greyhounds, sheep, cattle, pigs, rabbits, rats, moles, antelopes, fowl) vary widely; sample size, recording practice, age at which sex is recorded, and breeder perception bias affect reliability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin provides tabulated returns and anecdotal reports but warns of small samples and estimation biases (e.g., sex of sheep recorded at castration age not at birth). Use careful statistical consideration and account for mortality, recording age, and breeder practices when using such data.
